questions.stem: Which vector is perpendicular to the plane which contains the points $P(-1, -1, 1)$, $Q(1, 2, 3)$, and $R(3, 2, -1)$?
questions.solution:
A vector perpendicular to the plane is perpendicular to two vectors lying in it, so take their cross product. $\overrightarrow{PQ} = \langle 2, 3, 2 \rangle$ and $\overrightarrow{PR} = \langle 4, 3, -2 \rangle$, so

$$
\overrightarrow{PQ} \times \overrightarrow{PR} = \begin{vmatrix} \vec{i} & \vec{j} & \vec{k} \\ 2 & 3 & 2 \\ 4 & 3 & -2 \end{vmatrix} = \langle -12, 12, -6 \rangle = -6\langle 2, -2, 1 \rangle.
$$

So the vector perpendicular to the plane is $\langle 2, -2, 1 \rangle$, since any nonzero multiple of the normal is also normal.

questions.stem:
Which of the following are true and which are false?

(I) For every $\vec{u}$ and $\vec{v}$ the orthogonal vector projection of $\vec{u}$ onto $\vec{v}$, $\operatorname{proj}_{\vec{v}} \vec{u}$, is equal to the orthogonal vector projection of $\vec{u}$ onto $2\vec{v}$, $\operatorname{proj}_{2\vec{v}} \vec{u}$.

(II) $\vec{u} \cdot \vec{u} = |\vec{u}|^2$ for every vector $\vec{u}$.

(III) $(\vec{u} \times \vec{v}) \cdot \vec{v} = 0$ for every pair of vectors $\vec{u}$ and $\vec{v}$.
questions.solution:
(I) $\operatorname{proj}_{2\vec{v}} \vec{u} = \dfrac{\vec{u} \cdot 2\vec{v}}{|2\vec{v}|^2}\, 2\vec{v} = \dfrac{2\,\vec{u} \cdot \vec{v}}{4|\vec{v}|^2}\, 2\vec{v} = \dfrac{\vec{u} \cdot \vec{v}}{|\vec{v}|^2}\, \vec{v} = \operatorname{proj}_{\vec{v}} \vec{u}$, so (I) is true. Scaling $\vec{v}$ does not change the projection.

(II) $\vec{u} \cdot \vec{u} = |\vec{u}|^2$ is the definition of length squared, so (II) is true.

(III) $\vec{u} \times \vec{v}$ is perpendicular to $\vec{v}$, so $(\vec{u} \times \vec{v}) \cdot \vec{v} = 0$, and (III) is true.

All three statements are true.

questions.stem: Suppose $\vec{u} \cdot \vec{v} = \sqrt{3}$ and $\vec{u} \times \vec{v} = \langle 1, 2, 2 \rangle$. What is the angle between $\vec{u}$ and $\vec{v}$?
questions.solution:
Let $\theta$ be the angle between $\vec{u}$ and $\vec{v}$. Then $|\vec{u} \times \vec{v}| = |\vec{u}||\vec{v}|\sin\theta$ and $\vec{u} \cdot \vec{v} = |\vec{u}||\vec{v}|\cos\theta$. Dividing the first by the second gives

$$
\tan\theta = \frac{|\vec{u} \times \vec{v}|}{\vec{u} \cdot \vec{v}} = \frac{\sqrt{1 + 4 + 4}}{\sqrt{3}} = \frac{3}{\sqrt{3}} = \sqrt{3}.
$$

The dot product is positive, so $\theta$ is acute, and $\tan\theta = \sqrt{3}$ gives $\theta = \frac{\pi}{3}$.

questions.stem: Find the area of the region bounded by the curves $x = 4y - y^2$ and $x = y^2 - 2y$.
questions.solution:
The curves meet where $4y - y^2 = y^2 - 2y$, that is $2y^2 - 6y = 0$, so $y = 0$ or $y = 3$. For $0 \le y \le 3$ the curve $x = 4y - y^2$ lies to the right, since $(4y - y^2) - (y^2 - 2y) = 6y - 2y^2 \ge 0$. So the area is

$$
\int_0^3 (6y - 2y^2)\, dy = \left[3y^2 - \tfrac{2}{3}y^3\right]_0^3 = 27 - 18 = 9.
$$

So the area is $9$.

questions.stem: The region in the first quadrant bounded by the curves $y = x^2$ and $x = y$ is rotated about the axis $y = 0$. Find the volume of the resulting solid.
questions.solution:
The curves $y = x^2$ and $x = y$ meet at $(0,0)$ and $(1,1)$. For $0 \le x \le 1$ the line $y = x$ lies above the parabola, so the region is $x^2 \le y \le x$. Rotating about the $x$-axis gives washers with outer radius $x$ and inner radius $x^2$, so

$$
V = \pi \int_0^1 \left( x^2 - x^4 \right) dx = \pi \left( \frac{1}{3} - \frac{1}{5} \right) = \frac{2\pi}{15}.
$$

So the volume is $\frac{2\pi}{15}$.

questions.stem:
Evaluate the integral

$$
\int_0^1 x2^x dx.
$$
questions.solution:
Integrate by parts with $u = x$ and $dv = 2^x\, dx$, so $v = \dfrac{2^x}{\ln 2}$. Then

$$
\int_0^1 x2^x\, dx = \left[\frac{x 2^x}{\ln 2}\right]_0^1 - \frac{1}{\ln 2}\int_0^1 2^x\, dx = \frac{2}{\ln 2} - \frac{1}{\ln 2}\cdot\frac{1}{\ln 2},
$$

where $\int_0^1 2^x\, dx = \dfrac{2 - 1}{\ln 2}$. Combining over $(\ln 2)^2$ gives $\dfrac{2\ln 2 - 1}{(\ln 2)^2}$.

Taking $v = 2^x$ forgets the factor $\frac{1}{\ln 2}$, the usual slip with a base other than $e$.

questions.stem:
Evaluate the integral

$$
\int_2^3 \frac{2x+2}{x^2-x}dx.
$$
questions.solution:
Partial fractions: $\dfrac{2x + 2}{x(x-1)} = \dfrac{A}{x} + \dfrac{B}{x-1}$ gives $2x + 2 = A(x-1) + Bx$. Setting $x = 0$ gives $A = -2$, and setting $x = 1$ gives $B = 4$. So

$$
\int_2^3 \left( \frac{4}{x-1} - \frac{2}{x} \right) dx = \Big[ 4\ln(x-1) - 2\ln x \Big]_2^3 = (4\ln 2 - 2\ln 3) - (-2\ln 2) = 6\ln 2 - 2\ln 3.
$$

So the integral is $\ln\left(\frac{64}{9}\right)$.

questions.stem: Use the method of cylindrical shells to find the volume of the solid obtained by rotating the region bounded by the curves $y = x^3$, $y = 0$, and $x = 1$ about the line $x = 1$. Express your answer as a definite integral.
questions.solution:
Use shells. A vertical strip at position $x$, $0 \le x \le 1$, has height $x^3$, and the distance from the axis $x = 1$ is $1 - x$. Each shell has volume $2\pi(1-x)\,x^3\,dx$, so

$$
V = 2\pi \int_0^1 (1 - x)\, x^3\, dx.
$$

The radius is measured from $x = 1$, not from the $y$-axis, so using $x$ as the radius gives the wrong integrand.

questions.stem: A tank of height 10 m and whose horizontal cross sections are squares of side 2 m is filled with water. How much work is required to pump all of the water out of the tank? Assume that water has density $\rho$ kg/m$^3$ and that the acceleration due to gravity is $g$ m/s$^2$.
questions.solution:
Let $y$ be the depth below the top of the tank, $0 \le y \le 10$. A horizontal slice at depth $y$ has area $2^2 = 4$ and thickness $dy$, so its weight is $4\rho g\, dy$. Each slice must be lifted to the top, a distance $y$, so

$$
W = \int_0^{10} 4\rho g\, y\, dy = 4\rho g \left[\frac{y^2}{2}\right]_0^{10} = 200\rho g \text{ J}.
$$

The distance is measured up to the top of the tank, not down to the bottom, which would give a different answer.

questions.stem:
A trigonometric substitution can be used to convert the definite integral

$$
\int_2^5 \frac{dx}{\sqrt{x^2 - 4x + 13}}
$$

into which of the following definite integrals?
questions.solution: Complete the square: $x^2 - 4x + 13 = (x-2)^2 + 9$. Let $u = x - 2$, so the limits become $u = 0$ to $u = 3$ and the integral is $\displaystyle\int_0^3 \frac{du}{\sqrt{u^2 + 9}}$. Substitute $u = 3\tan\theta$, so $du = 3\sec^2\theta\, d\theta$ and $\sqrt{u^2 + 9} = 3\sec\theta$. The integrand becomes $\sec\theta\, d\theta$, with $\theta$ running from $0$ to $\frac{\pi}{4}$. So the integral is $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/4} \sec\theta\, d\theta$.

questions.stem: A swimming pool 100 m long, 10 m wide and 2 m deep is filled with water. Calculate the total force against a wall that has dimensions 10 m by 2 m. Assume that water has density $\rho$ kg/m$^3$ and that the acceleration due to gravity is $g$ m/s$^2$.
questions.solution:
Let $d$ be the depth below the surface, $0 \le d \le 2$. The wall is $10$ m wide, so a horizontal strip at depth $d$ has area $10\, dd$ and pressure $\rho g d$. The force is

$$
F = \int_0^2 \rho g\, d \cdot 10\, dd = 10\rho g \left[\frac{d^2}{2}\right]_0^2 = 20\rho g \text{ N}.
$$

The $100$ m length of the pool plays no part, since only the wall is involved.

questions.stem:
Evaluate the improper integral if it converges. If it does not converge, state that it diverges.

$$
\int_0^{\pi/2} \tan(\theta)\, d\theta.
$$
questions.solution:
The integrand $\tan\theta$ is unbounded as $\theta \to \frac{\pi}{2}^-$, so the integral is improper and must be written as a limit:

$$
\int_0^{\pi/2} \tan\theta\, d\theta = \lim_{b \to \pi/2^-} \left[-\ln|\cos\theta|\right]_0^b = \lim_{b \to \pi/2^-} \left(-\ln \cos b\right).
$$

Since $\cos b \to 0^+$, $-\ln\cos b \to \infty$, so the integral diverges. Evaluating the antiderivative at the endpoint without the limit is the trap.

questions.stem: Compute the surface area of the solid obtained by rotating the curve $y = \frac{1}{3}x^3$, $0 \le x \le 1$, about the x-axis. Express your answer as a definite integral.
questions.solution:
For $y = \frac{x^3}{3}$, $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = x^2$. Rotating about the $x$-axis, the radius is $y$, so the surface area is

$$
S = 2\pi \int_0^1 y \sqrt{1 + \left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)^2}\, dx = 2\pi \int_0^1 \frac{x^3}{3}\sqrt{1 + x^4}\, dx = \frac{2\pi}{3} \int_0^1 x^3 \sqrt{x^4 + 1}\, dx.
$$

The $\frac{1}{3}$ from $y$ stays in front of the integral.

questions.stem: Find the sum of telescopic series $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n^2+n}$
questions.solution:
Factor the denominator and split by partial fractions: $\dfrac{1}{n^2 + n} = \dfrac{1}{n(n+1)} = \dfrac{1}{n} - \dfrac{1}{n+1}$. The partial sums telescope:

$$
s_N = \sum_{n=1}^{N} \left( \frac{1}{n} - \frac{1}{n+1} \right) = 1 - \frac{1}{N+1}.
$$

As $N \to \infty$, $s_N \to 1$, so the sum is $1$.

questions.stem:
Test the following series for convergence:

(I) $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \ln\left(1 + \frac{1}{n^2}\right)$

(II) $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \sin\left(\frac{1}{n}\right)$

(III) $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} (\sqrt{n^3} - \sqrt{n^3 - 1})$

choices.label: A
choices.text: I is convergent; II and III are divergent.

choices.label: B
choices.text: I and III are convergent; II is divergent.

choices.label: C
choices.text: I and III are divergent; II is convergent.

choices.label: D
choices.text: I, II and III are divergent.

choices.label: E
choices.text: I, II and II are convergent.

questions.solution:
(I) $0 < \ln\left(1 + \frac{1}{n^2}\right) \le \frac{1}{n^2}$, and $\sum \frac{1}{n^2}$ converges, so (I) converges.

(II) $\lim_{n \to \infty} \dfrac{\sin(1/n)}{1/n} = 1$, and $\sum \frac{1}{n}$ diverges, so by the limit comparison test (II) diverges.

(III) $\sqrt{n^3} - \sqrt{n^3 - 1} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{n^3} + \sqrt{n^3 - 1}} \le \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{n^3}} = n^{-3/2}$, and the $p$-series with $p = \frac{3}{2} > 1$ converges, so (III) converges.

So (I) and (III) converge and (II) diverges. The difference in (III) must be rationalised before comparing; comparing the two square roots directly does not give a usable bound.

questions.stem:
Represent $\int_0^1 \cos x^2 dx$ as an infinite series.

Hint: $\cos x = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} (-1)^k \frac{x^{2k}}{(2k)!}$
questions.solution:
Replace $x$ by $x^2$ in the series for $\cos x$: $\cos x^2 = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} (-1)^k \dfrac{x^{4k}}{(2k)!}$. Integrate term by term from $0$ to $1$, using $\int_0^1 x^{4k}\, dx = \dfrac{1}{4k+1}$:

$$
\int_0^1 \cos x^2\, dx = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^k}{(2k)!\,(4k+1)}.
$$

The factor $(2k)!$ stays in the denominator, since only the power of $x$ changes on integration.

questions.stem: Compute the power series that represents $\frac{1}{(1+2x)^2}$
questions.solution:
Differentiate the geometric series $\dfrac{1}{1 - t} = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} t^k$ to get $\dfrac{1}{(1-t)^2} = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} k\, t^{k-1}$. Put $t = -2x$, so $1 - t = 1 + 2x$:

$$
\frac{1}{(1+2x)^2} = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} k(-2x)^{k-1} = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} k(-2)^{k-1} x^{k-1}.
$$

The substitution must be $t = -2x$, not $2x$, which is why the alternating signs appear.

questions.stem: The first three terms of the Maclaurin series for $f(x) = (1+3x)^{-\frac{1}{3}}$ are
questions.solution:
Write $f(x) = (1 + u)^{-1/3}$ with $u = 3x$. The binomial series gives

$$
(1 + u)^{-1/3} = 1 - \frac{1}{3}u + \frac{\left(-\frac{1}{3}\right)\left(-\frac{4}{3}\right)}{2}u^2 + \cdots = 1 - \frac{1}{3}u + \frac{2}{9}u^2 + \cdots.
$$

With $u = 3x$, $-\frac{1}{3}u = -x$ and $\frac{2}{9}u^2 = 2x^2$, so the first three terms are $1 - x + 2x^2$.

Leaving the $3$ out of $u = 3x$ gives $1 - \frac{1}{3}x + \frac{2}{9}x^2$, the usual slip.

questions.stem: Suppose we want to approximate the sum of the series $\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^k}{k^3}$ by the sum $s_m = \sum_{k=1}^{m} \frac{(-1)^k}{k^3}$ of the first $m$ terms. By the theory of alternating series, the error will be less than or equal to $10^{-3}$ provided $m =$
questions.solution:
The terms $\frac{1}{k^3}$ decrease to $0$, so the alternating series estimation theorem bounds the error after $m$ terms by the first omitted term: $|R_m| \le \dfrac{1}{(m+1)^3}$. We need $\dfrac{1}{(m+1)^3} \le 10^{-3}$, so $(m+1)^3 \ge 1000$ and $m + 1 \ge 10$, giving $m \ge 9$. Check: $m = 8$ gives $\frac{1}{729} > 10^{-3}$, so $m = 9$ is the smallest value.

Bounding by $\frac{1}{m^3}$ instead of $\frac{1}{(m+1)^3}$ wrongly gives $m = 10$.

questions.stem: The equation $4\cos\theta + \sin\theta = \frac{2}{r}$ in polar coordinates represents a part of

choices.label: D
choices.text: an ellipse which is not a circle

questions.solution:
Multiply both sides by $r$: $4r\cos\theta + r\sin\theta = 2$. With $x = r\cos\theta$ and $y = r\sin\theta$, this becomes $4x + y = 2$, so $y = 2 - 4x$.

This is a straight line, and the whole line is traced out.

questions.stem:
What is the length of arc of the spiral given in polar coordinates by

$$
r = e^{-2\theta}, 0 \le \theta \le 1/2?
$$
questions.solution:
For a polar curve, $L = \int_a^b \sqrt{r^2 + (r')^2}\, d\theta$. Here $r = e^{-2\theta}$ and $r' = -2e^{-2\theta}$, so $r^2 + (r')^2 = 5e^{-4\theta}$ and $\sqrt{r^2 + (r')^2} = \sqrt{5}\, e^{-2\theta}$. Then

$$
L = \sqrt{5} \int_0^{1/2} e^{-2\theta}\, d\theta = \sqrt{5}\left[-\frac{e^{-2\theta}}{2}\right]_0^{1/2} = \frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}\left(1 - e^{-1}\right) = \frac{(e-1)\sqrt{5}}{2e}.
$$

Dropping the $(r')^2$ term loses the factor $\sqrt{5}$.

Split the term into two geometric pieces: $\dfrac{3 + 2^n}{4^n} = 3\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)^n + \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^n$. Each sum starts at $n = 1$:

$$
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} 3\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^n = 3 \cdot \frac{1/4}{1 - 1/4} = 1, \qquad \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^n = \frac{1/2}{1 - 1/2} = 1.
$$

So the total is $1 + 1 = 2$. Starting the sums at $n = 0$ would add an extra $3 + 1 = 4$.

questions.stem:
For which of the following series the ratio test is inconclusive?

(I) $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{7^n}{n!}$

(II) $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n^2}$

(III) $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{\ln n}{n}$
questions.solution:
The ratio test is inconclusive when $\lim_{n \to \infty} \left|\dfrac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}\right| = 1$.

(I) $\dfrac{7^{n+1}/(n+1)!}{7^n/n!} = \dfrac{7}{n+1} \to 0$, so the test is conclusive.

(II) $\dfrac{1/(n+1)^2}{1/n^2} = \left(\dfrac{n}{n+1}\right)^2 \to 1$, so the test is inconclusive.

(III) $\dfrac{\ln(n+1)/(n+1)}{\ln n/n} = \dfrac{n}{n+1} \cdot \dfrac{\ln(n+1)}{\ln n} \to 1 \cdot 1 = 1$, so the test is inconclusive.

So the ratio test is inconclusive for (II) and (III).

questions.stem: The area between the spirals $r = \theta$ and $r = 2\theta$, $0 \le \theta \le \pi/2$ is
questions.solution:
At each angle $\theta$ with $0 \le \theta \le \frac{\pi}{2}$, the region lies between $r = \theta$ (inner) and $r = 2\theta$ (outer). The area is

$$
A = \frac{1}{2}\int_0^{\pi/2} \left( (2\theta)^2 - \theta^2 \right) d\theta = \frac{3}{2}\int_0^{\pi/2} \theta^2\, d\theta = \frac{3}{2} \cdot \frac{1}{3}\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)^3 = \frac{\pi^3}{16}.
$$

The outer curve must be the larger one, $r = 2\theta$; swapping them gives a negative integrand.

questions.stem:
Which is true? The point whose Cartesian coordinates are $(1, \sqrt{3})$ has polar coordinates

I. $(2, \pi/3)$

II. $(2, -5\pi/3)$

III. $(2, 4\pi/3)$
questions.solution:
The point $(1, \sqrt{3})$ has $r = \sqrt{1 + 3} = 2$ and, since it lies in the first quadrant with $\tan\theta = \sqrt{3}$, $\theta = \frac{\pi}{3}$. Check each representation:

(I) $(2, \frac{\pi}{3})$ is the given point.

(II) $(2, -\frac{5\pi}{3})$ differs from $\frac{\pi}{3}$ by $-2\pi$, so it is the same point.

(III) $(2, \frac{4\pi}{3})$ gives $\left(2\cos\frac{4\pi}{3}, 2\sin\frac{4\pi}{3}\right) = (-1, -\sqrt{3})$, a different point. Its angle is $\pi$ away, which would need $r = -2$ rather than $r = 2$.

So only (I) and (II) are true.
